summary:
Hursh Agrawal, CTO of The Browser Company, argues that the manager schedule is now usable as building time thanks to autonomous coding agents. Despite 15+ recurring meetings, seven direct reports, and a toddler, he consistently ships 2–10 PRs per week — something not possible several months ago. Three reasons make building necessary for leaders: frontier models turnover every ~3 months and can only be calibrated through hands-on use; showing a working prototype beats arguing about capability each quarter; and leaders' business context makes their per-token steering of agents more valuable than an IC's. Agents are strong at execution but weak at judgment, and delegation skills transfer directly.

He outlines a daily shape of 2–3 hours of coding — a morning review block, short steering blocks between meetings, and a critical 5pm setup block — feeding an overnight agent loop. He walks through three overnight patterns. First, building a feature: a co-worker agent assembles context into a prompt, a coding agent writes tests first, verifies end-to-end with computer use, splits into reviewer-friendly PRs, runs AI code review, gets CI green, and leaves a morning report. Second, hill-climbing AI features: a feedback button collects a handful (4–30) of JSON dumps, the overnight run turns them into an eval set, designs scoring functions, runs a harness, and hill-climps until scores improve — saving the flow as a reusable skill. Third, training a small model (e.g., a BERT PII classifier): business context plus training data, synthetic-data bolstering, ensemble of frontier models, train two candidates in an AWS sandbox (never prod), test against evals, deprovision, and report — including inference hosting instructions.

The caveats are real. The system only works on top of organizational scaffolding: AI code review, agents.md / claude.md hygiene, trustworthy CI, sophisticated feature flags, and a prototype branch for employees. His own code has caused SEVs. Tactical hygiene matters: test everything yourself before the PR goes up, keep PRs small and readable to model good behavior for the team, and never add other reviewers to code you have not read. His closing call is to push task scope — give agents weeks-to-months of work overnight — and let that capability surface new product ideas for the team.

takeaways: The manager schedule is now usable as building time thanks to autonomous coding agents; building is part of the leadership job, not optional.
Frontier models turnover roughly every three months, so leaders must build hands-on to calibrate capabilities instead of relaying Twitter opinions.
Showing a working prototype to engineers is far more efficient than arguing about what a new model can do each quarter.
Leaders are well-suited to drive agents because their business context makes per-token steering more valuable than an IC's.
A 5pm setup block feeds an overnight agent loop that returns shippable, review-ready work — for features, eval hill-climbing, and small-model training.

Eval hill-climbing: collect a handful of feedback JSON dumps, ask the agent overnight to build an eval set, design scoring functions, and hill-climb until scores improve — saving the flow as a reusable skill.

Training small models overnight works: give the agent business context, training data, an ensemble of frontier models for synthetic data, an AWS sandbox (never prod), and have it train two candidates and report.
Organizational scaffolding — trustworthy CI, feature flags, a prototype branch, AI code review, agents.md/claude.md hygiene — is what makes overnight prototyping safe.
Tactical hygiene: test every overnight result yourself, keep PRs small and readable to model good behavior, and never add reviewers to code you have not read.
Push task scope deliberately — give agents weeks-to-months of work overnight to discover what frontier models are really capable of.

sections.title: A manager's calendar, and why building became the job
sections.summary: Hursh introduces himself, shows his actual calendar with 15+ recurring meetings and seven direct reports, and reports shipping 2–10 PRs per week despite a toddler and a 40–50 hour week. He argues the manager schedule is now usable as building time and that building has become part of the leader's job.

sections.title: Judging a new model, and showing rather than arguing
sections.summary: Frontier models change every few months; leaders cannot tell what a new model is good for without hands-on use, and intuition is hard to communicate. Showing engineers a working prototype beats arguing about capability each quarter, and leaders' business context makes their steering more valuable per token than an IC's.

sections.title: Execution is solved, judgment is not
sections.summary: Agents are strong at execution but weaker at judgment; leaders can coach them past premature 'this is impossible' conclusions. Delegation skills — goals, context, check-ins, coaching — transfer directly to agent management. He defers to Julie Zhuo's taxonomy of what leaders should build.

sections.title: Four things leaders should build, and one to avoid
sections.summary: Four categories: internal tools, celebration artifacts for the team, vision prototypes using new model families, and artifacts to push product/business boundaries. He explicitly warns against taking critical-path work that depends on the leader, who will get pulled into fires and recruiting calls.

sections.title: The daily shape, and why 5pm matters most
sections.summary: Two to three hours of coding per day: a morning review block for last night's output, short steering blocks between meetings, and the critical 5pm setup block that initiates the overnight run — whether coding, training models, or hill-climbing prompts.

sections.title: Building a feature overnight, and assembling the prompt
sections.summary: Mindset shift: give the agent all the context you would need to make decisions, since you won't be there overnight. Use a co-worker agent to spend ~20 minutes assembling a context-rich prompt from Slack, Jira, Notion, and the repo, then paste it into the coding agent with instructions to implement the feature.

sections.title: Verification, PR hygiene, and the morning report
sections.summary: Prompt the agent to write tests first, verify the end-to-end flow with computer use, split work into reviewer-friendly PRs, run AI code review in a clean sub-agent, get CI green, resolve bot comments, and leave a morning report on trade-offs and status. Modern models compress weeks of work into one overnight run, producing a 'little present' each morning.

sections.title: Hill climbing a feature from a few feedback dumps
sections.summary: Prototyping loop: add a feedback button to an AI feature, collect 4–30 JSON dumps across the day, then at 5pm hand them to the agent to build an eval set (SQLite/Markdown), design scoring functions interactively, build a hill-climbing harness, run overnight, and save the flow as a reusable skill. Even small eval sets yield non-overfit improvements that ship to employees and production.

sections.title: Training a classifier overnight
sections.summary: Brief the agent with business context and collected training data; have it clean and bolster with synthetic data using an ensemble of frontier models, provision an AWS sandbox (never prod), pick the right GPU/EC2, train two candidate models, test against evals, deprovision, and leave a morning report — including how to host inference. Worked on a BERT PII classifier where Opus/Haiku were expensive and weak on precision/recall.

sections.title: Pushing task scope, and the scaffolding it needs
sections.summary: Push task scope deliberately — give agents weeks-to-months of work overnight to discover what frontier models are really capable of (echoing Simon Lass's tweet). Caveat: this only works on top of organizational scaffolding — AI code review, agents.md/claude.md hygiene, trustworthy CI, sophisticated feature flags, and a prototype branch that goes to employees but not production. His own code has caused SEVs.

sections.title: Never add reviewers to code you have not read
sections.summary: Tactical hygiene: test every overnight result yourself in the morning slot, keep PRs small and readable because you are modeling good behavior for the team, and never add other reviewers to code you have not read — senior engineers will call you out. Closing: building is part of the job now, doable in one or two hours a day, and you will automatically surface new product ideas by exercising the capability.

demonstrations: Building a feature overnight via a context-rich prompt assembled by a co-worker agent and executed by a coding agent, with test-first, computer-use verification, AI code review, and a morning report
Hill-climbing an AI feature from 4–30 feedback JSON dumps: agent builds an eval set, designs scoring functions, runs a harness, and hill-climps overnight — saving the flow as a reusable skill

Training a BERT PII classifier overnight: agent cleans training data, bolsters with synthetic data from an ensemble of frontier models, provisions an AWS sandbox, trains two candidates, evaluates, deprovisions, and reports — including inference hosting instructions
Using the hill-climb pattern internally for an internal code-reviewer feature to improve quality
limitations: Requires organizational scaffolding: trustworthy CI, feature flags, a prototype branch, AI code review, agents.md/claude.md hygiene
Leader code has caused SEVs and annoyed engineers — 'you will get humbled'
Should not take critical-path work dependent on the leader
Agent execution is strong but judgment still requires human steering — models often prematurely declare tasks impossible
Test-writing after the fact is sloppier than test-first
Overfitting on small eval sets is a real risk — must explicitly tell the agent not to overfit
Whether 'encouraging' prompts help the agent is admitted as uncertain
Do not give the agent production AWS access — always use a sandbox
Never add other reviewers to code you have not read yourself
